report.body_markdown:
# Research Report

**Goal:** Compare the current evidence on LFP and high-nickel NMC battery chemistries for passenger EVs, focusing on cycle life, energy density, thermal safety, cost drivers, and how pack-level engineering changes the practical trade-off. Prefer peer-reviewed work, DOE or national lab reports, and credible manufacturer engineering data.

## Questions
- (answered) Investigate cell-level performance metrics, degradation mechanisms, cycle life, and thermal runaway characteristics of LFP versus high-nickel NMC chemistries using peer-reviewed studies and DOE/national laboratory technical reports.
- (answered) Analyze direct material, processing, and supply-chain cost drivers for LFP versus high-nickel NMC cells, covering raw material price sensitivities (Li, Ni, Co, Fe, P) and total $/kWh economics from credible industry and lab reports.
- (answered) Evaluate how pack-level engineering innovations (Cell-to-Pack, blade form factors, structural integration, and thermal barrier mitigation) offset cell-level deficits and reshape practical commercial EV platform trade-offs between LFP and high-nickel NMC.

## Synthesis
Adopt a segmented EV battery strategy: utilize LFP chemistries for standard-range, cost-sensitive, and high-durability vehicle segments, while reserving high-nickel NMC chemistries for long-range and premium performance platforms where gravimetric energy density is paramount.

Empirical and technical data show distinct performance trade-offs between LFP and NMC chemistries. High-nickel NMC achieves superior cell-level specific energy (200–280 Wh/kg) and pack-level specific energy (140–200 Wh/kg), maximizing driving range in weight-constrained applications. However, NMC exhibits lower thermal stability, with thermal runaway onset between ~150–210°C, substantial oxygen release during failure, and higher toxic gas emissions, necessitating complex active thermal management systems and battery management system (BMS) controls. In contrast, LFP displays substantially superior thermal safety with a thermal runaway threshold of ~270–300°C, minimal oxygen release, reduced propagation risk, and lower raw material costs, though at the expense of lower specific energy.
